newsitem.title: USA: New England officials target Midwest polluters.
newsitem.headline: New England officials target Midwest polluters.

text.p: Officials in Maine and Massachusetts are urging Northeastern states to band together and target pollution from Midwestern coal-fired power plants they blame for much of the region's air problems.

Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger and Maine Gov. Angus King have seperately proposed that the 12 Northeast states and the District of Columbia form what Harshbarger is calling a "Northeast Clean Air Compact."
In a letter sent to the region's governors, Harshbarger proposed Tuesday that the Northeastern states ban or place a surcharge on power from Midwestern states that allow dirty plants to operate.

The letter is the latest in a long battle between the coal-producing Midwestern states and the downwind Eastern states where officials contend more than half of the pollution is caused by outside sources.
Harshbarger said he feared the situation could worsen with deregulation of the power industry, and as demand for power from lower-cost coal plants increases.

"Today's proposal fires a strong message to the Midwestern power plants and the states themselves that they should not expect to be able to compete in the big Northeast power market unless they clean up their act," Harshbarger said in a statement.
King, a former energy consultant who sent a similar letter to the governors last month, said it was important for the Northeastern states to present a unified front on the issue of air quality.

"Fundamentally it just does not make common sense to allow plants in the Midwest that don't meet environmental requirements of the rest of the country to gear up and double their output of power sending us lousy air at the same time," King told reporters.
James Milkey, the chief of the environmental policies for the Massachusetts attorney general's office, said his state was frustrated by federal measures to try to stem air pollution.
"The goal obviously is to clean our air," Milkey said. "We can't really do that without holding the big Midwestern power plants to modern environmental standards."

The proposal for the Northeastern states to band together has drawn opposition from some Midwestern political leaders, and at least one New England environmental group has said it would oppose the plan.

"Basically what this is, is an effort by the Northeast states to ban together... to point a finger at somebody else for a pollution problem that is in part caused by their own actions," Rusty Russell, a staff attorney for the Conservation Law Foundation, told Maine Public Radio.
Rusell expressed concern that the proposal might violate laws protecting interstate commerce, but Milkey said that obstacle could be overcome.
King said he will take up the issue at the Dec. 13, meeting of the Council of Northeastern Governors in Vermont.
